name: Sprintz
baseline: Simple8b, FastPFor, SIMD-BP128 (also LZ4HC, Brotli, Blosc, FSE, LZO in the author's wider runs)
workload: Compression ratio and single-thread decompression speed on quantized 8-bit and 16-bit multivariate integer time series (AMPDs, MSRC-12, PAMAP, UCI Gas, UCR archive), against general and integer codecs run through the author's lzbench fork.
claimed_speedup: README: 'state-of-the-art compression ratios, and can decompress at multiple GB/s in a single thread'; also 'does even better relative to other methods' with 1KB and 10KB blocks. Raw numbers are in the repo results/ directory; no per-codec table on the README page (not opened).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in README; it says only 'tested with Clang on OS X'
tradeoffs: Built for small-memory streaming of integer time series (a few bytes of state per variable), not for sorted posting lists. Benchmarks need Python, joblib, pandas and the separate dblalock/lzbench fork. Only tested with Clang on macOS.
caveats: Benchmark harness and result files live in a separate repo (dblalock/lzbench) and the results/ directory; I did not open the numbers themselves, and the paper (arXiv, ACM) is blocked in this environment. FastPFor, SIMD-BP128 and Simple8b were run on 8/16-bit data zero-padded to 32 bits (README says so) and compression ratios were divided by the padding factor, which favours the byte-aware Sprintz. README states the speed claim without CPU model or flags, so tier is B (peer-reviewed) rather than A. Last commit date taken from the github.com commits page; a search snippet said the repo was updated in May 2024.

name: bitpacking (quickwit-oss, Rust port of simdcomp)
baseline: scalar bit-packing (its own BitPacker1x scalar-layout packer); README names no external incumbent
workload: Compress/decompress (and delta variants) of blocks of 32, 128 or 256 u32 values, single thread, via cargo bench.
claimed_speedup: BitPacker1x: compress 1.4 billion int/s, decompress 1.8 billion int/s. BitPacker4x (SSE3): compress 5.3, decompress 5.5, decompress_delta 5 billion int/s. BitPacker8x (AVX2): compress 7, decompress 6.5, decompress_delta 5.6 billion int/s. README headline: 'Expect > 4 billions integers per seconds.' Ratio SSE3 or AVX2 over BitPacker1x is roughly 3-5x (derived from page data).
stars_or_usage: 341 stars; used by tantivy (not verified on the page I opened)
tradeoffs: Rust crate, not callable from C++ without a C wrapper. BitPacker1x/4x/8x formats are mutually incompatible. Runtime fallback to scalar when SSE3/AVX2 are missing.
caveats: No head-to-head against FastPFor, simdcomp, varint or Simple8b is shown on the page; the only comparison is among its own three layouts and a remark that LZ4 is a poor fit. It is a port of Lemire's simdcomp, so it adds portability to Rust rather than a new algorithm. Compiler flags not given. Tantivy usage not confirmed from a page I opened.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'github SIMD bit packing library benchmark faster than simdcomp FastPFor AVX-512 ...' and the FastPFor README related-project list

name: go-simd/bitpack
baseline: scalar Go bit-packer (the package's own scalar reference); output is byte-identical to Lemire's simdcomp, which is not benchmarked
workload: Pack and unpack blocks of 128 uint32 values at bit widths 8, 16 and 24 with Go assembly kernels (SSE2/AVX2 on amd64, VSX on ppc64le, vector facility on s390x), CI runs with -count=6.
claimed_speedup: amd64 CI (AVX2): Pack ~62.0 GB/s vs scalar ~2.31 GB/s at 8 bits; Unpack ~44.5 GB/s vs ~2.08 GB/s at 8 bits; overall '~21-32x over scalar'. Re-bench on a QEMU VM: ~17.8-20.1x pack, ~18.3-24.0x unpack. POWER9 VSX bits=8: Pack ~7.0x, Unpack ~11.3x. IBM z15: Pack ~23x, Unpack ~34x.
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.26.4 stated for the POWER9 run; flags not stated; amd64 run on ubuntu-latest CI with -count=6
hardware: amd64 GitHub Actions runner (CPU model not stated), POWER9 (GCC Compile Farm), IBM z15; QEMU VM for the re-bench
tradeoffs: Go, so not directly usable from C++ (format is simdcomp-compatible, so a Go service can exchange data with a C++ simdcomp/FastPFor user). 128-value blocks only; arm64 has no SIMD kernel yet (scalar).
caveats: Baseline is the library's own scalar code, not simdcomp, FastPFor, varint or Simple8b. README says a head-to-head against ronanh/intcomp is only a follow-up. amd64 CI numbers come from shared runners with no CPU model, and the author's own QEMU re-bench gives lower ratios. Absolute GB/s figures are over the uint32 input stream.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'integer-bitpacking benchmark simdcomp FastPFor' result list (go-simd bitpack page)

name: LeCo (Learn-to-Compress)
baseline: Frame of Reference (FOR), Delta (fixed and variable), Elias-Fano
workload: Microbenchmarks of learned lightweight compression (regression-based serial-correlation model plus bit-packed residuals) of integer columns versus FOR, Delta and Elias-Fano, covering compression ratio and random-access/decode speed; datasets download via script.
claimed_speedup: No numbers on the repo page I opened. A search snippet of the SIGMOD'24 paper says LeCo gives a Pareto improvement over existing integer-compression algorithms (snippet only; paper blocked).
compiler_and_flags: CMake build on Ubuntu 20.04.4 LTS; flags not stated on the page
tradeoffs: Targets column stores (ratio plus random access) rather than raw bit-packing throughput. Needs Python-generated scripts and downloaded datasets; two datasets need manual Kaggle download.
caveats: No license stated on the repo page (so usability reference). Baselines are FOR/Delta/Elias-Fano written inside the repo, not FastPFor, simdcomp or Simple8b. Speed and ratio numbers could not be read here; entry rests on the repo description plus a search snippet. Claim is mainly about compression ratio at comparable speed.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'LeCo lightweight compression learning serial correlations github code repository' (limited to github.com)

name: SFVInt
baseline: Facebook Folly and Google Protobuf LEB128 varint decoders
workload: Decoding LEB128 varints using BMI2 (PDEP/PEXT), about 500 lines of code, on Intel m6i instances.
claimed_speedup: 'up to 2x' decoding speedup over Folly and Google Protobuf (search snippet of the paper; not read from the paper itself)
tradeoffs: Needs BMI2 (Intel Haswell+, AMD Zen). Decodes one LEB128 varint at a time, not a SIMD batch format.
caveats: Snippet only: arXiv and ACM are blocked here and I found no code repository, so the numbers and hardware could not be checked. Entry is a paper without confirmed code.
